---
title: "Reading the published archive"
---

opus publishes the four Tier-1 exchange tables as parquet at
[`heima.hafro.is/~einarhj/datras/raw`](https://heima.hafro.is/~einarhj/datras/raw),
converted from ICES's ASMX XML service. The files are not the interesting part
— **each one carries its own dictionary in its footer**, so a file that has been
copied, renamed or emailed still knows what its columns mean, what the legacy
ICES name for each was, which sentinels were stripped from it, and which known
ICES issues affect it.

This page is how to read that. Everything below runs against the published
files over https, with opus installed and nothing else set up.

| Table | Rows | Columns | Footer metadata |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **HH** Haul information | 150,217 | 69 | 90 KB |
| **HL** Length frequency | 14,423,771 | 29 | 65 KB |
| **CA** Catch at age | 5,968,027 | 34 | 67 KB |
| **LT** Litter assessment | 79,451 | 58 | 74 KB |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Outputs on this page were captured from the published archive on 2026-08-30.
The shapes are stable; the counts move whenever the archive is rebuilt.
:::

## Point at it

```r
library(opus)
options(opus.archive = "https://heima.hafro.is/~einarhj/datras/raw")
```

That is the whole setup. Every accessor also takes `path =` if you would rather
be explicit, and `op_archive()` falls back to a local staging directory when one
exists, so the same code works against a local build and the published twin.

**Nothing is downloaded.** Each metadata call is a parquet footer read: DuckDB
issues one HTTP range request and fetches the footer, not the file. The first
costs about 0.4 seconds and is cached for the session — reading every accessor
on this page, for one table, takes under a second against an 84 MB file.

## What a file says about itself

```r
op_keys("HH")
#>                   key bytes
#> 1     datras:coverage 15925
#> 2         datras:dict 59654
#> 3 datras:known_issues  8149
#> 4   datras:provenance   432
#> 5    datras:sentinels  6175
```

Five keys. `op_provenance()` answers "where did this file come from", which
matters because the answer is checkable rather than assumed:

```r
t(op_provenance("HL"))
#> n_rows        "14423771"
#> n_cols        "29"
#> source        "ICES DATRAS ASMX web service"
#> built_utc     "2026-08-29T19:20:19Z"
#> opus_version  "0.2.0"
#> opus_git_sha  "00d9b7f"
#> dict_sha256   "d74c9e38cca9e46af89acdd80f6171e0b4754f6f06d3a1a85d68422a49562f48"
#> data_dict_cli "data-dict 0.0.3"
#> writer        "nanoparquet 0.5.1"
#> pipeline      "archive_02_download -> ... -> archive_06_consolidate"
```

The git sha and the dictionary's sha256 are both there, so a file can be tied
to the exact code and the exact specification that produced it.

## The dictionary

```r
op_dict("HH")[1:8, c("name", "legacy_name", "type", "parquet_type", "r_type", "units")]
#>             name legacy_name             type parquet_type    r_type units
#> 1   RecordHeader  RecordType             enum   BYTE_ARRAY character  <NA>
#> 2         Survey      Survey           string   BYTE_ARRAY character  <NA>
#> 3        Quarter     Quarter  number(ordinal)        INT32   integer  <NA>
#> 4        Country     Country           string   BYTE_ARRAY character  <NA>
#> 5       Platform        Ship           string   BYTE_ARRAY character  <NA>
#> 6           Gear        Gear             enum   BYTE_ARRAY character  <NA>
#> 7    SweepLength   SweepLngt number(quantity)        INT32   integer     m
#> 8 GearExceptions      GearEx             enum   BYTE_ARRAY character  <NA>
```

69 columns × 13 attributes for HH, including `label`, `description`,
`constraints` and the declared range.

**Three type views per column, deliberately.** `type` is opus's curated
*semantic* type, `parquet_type`/`logical_type` are what is physically stored,
and `r_type` is what a reader actually gets back. They are allowed to disagree:
`SweepLength` above is `number(quantity)` in the specification and INT32 on
disk. That is not a defect — the specification's types are deliberately coarser
than storage types — but a consumer that treats the curated `type` as a casting
instruction will manufacture a divergence the data does not have. Cast from
`r_type` or `parquet_type`; see [Approach](approach.qmd) for the reasoning.

## Names

DATRAS fields have two names — ICES's legacy on-the-wire names and the current
ones. The archive is published under current names and carries the mapping:

```r
op_crosswalk("CA") |> head(5)
#>     old_name     new_name
#> 1 RecordType RecordHeader
#> 2     Survey       Survey
#> 3    Quarter      Quarter
#> 4    Country      Country
#> 5       Ship     Platform
```

No external list is involved: the crosswalk is read from the same file as the
data, so it cannot describe a different vintage of the archive than the one you
loaded. `op_crosswalk()` refuses to return a mapping that is not total and
bijective, because a partial one is worse than none — an un-renamed column
would pass through looking translated.

`op_rename()` applies it in either direction, which is what you want when
handing results to someone who works in ICES's wire vocabulary:

```r
library(dplyr)

op_con("HH") |>
  filter(Survey == "DWS", Year == 2009) |>
  select(Survey, Year, StationName, HaulNumber, HaulValidity) |>
  head(3) |> collect() |>
  op_rename("HH", to = "legacy")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 5
#>   Survey  Year StNo  HaulNo HaulVal
#> 1 DWS     2009 2          2 V
#> 2 DWS     2009 4          4 V
#> 3 DWS     2009 5          5 V
```

## Codes

13 of HH's columns are enums, with 205 code/label pairs between them:

```r
op_enums("HH", "HaulValidity")
#>         column code                                                     label
#> 1 HaulValidity    A Additional valid stations not used for index calculations
#> 2 HaulValidity    C                                    Calibrated (BITS only)
#> 3 HaulValidity    I                                              Invalid haul
#> 4 HaulValidity    M                        Pelagic Midwater Trawl (BITS only)
#> 5 HaulValidity    N                                     No oxygen (BITS only)
#> 6 HaulValidity    S                                             Standard haul
#> 7 HaulValidity    V                                                 Valid haul
```

## Sentinels, and why the codes matter

DATRAS uses `-9` for "not recorded". opus strips it to `NA` where it means
absence — but not everywhere, and the file records which:

```r
s <- op_sentinel_meta("HH")
attr(s, "sentinel")   #> "-9"
attr(s, "meaning")    #> "Not recorded / not applicable"
s[s$action != "strip", ]$field
#> "DataType" "Tickler"
```

Two of HH's 69 columns keep their `-9`, because there it is a **documented real
answer** rather than a missing value:

```r
op_enums("HH", "Tickler") |> head(3)   # 32 codes in all, -9 through 30
#>    column code                   label
#> 1 Tickler   -9 No ticklers are allowed
#> 2 Tickler    0           Zero ticklers
#> 3 Tickler    1             One tickler
```

This is the case worth remembering. `Tickler = -9` is indistinguishable from a
missing value by inspection — same literal, similar frequency — and only the
vocabulary shipped in the footer tells them apart. Blanket `-9 → NA` on this
column destroys a real observation. The same overloading across other fields is
one of opus's open reports to ICES; see [Issues found](issues.qmd).

## What is known to be wrong with the table

```r
op_known_issues("CA")[, c("id", "severity", "field")]
#>                                  id      severity          field
#> 1    sentinel_replacement_data_loss opus-internal  all numeric columns
#> 2        ca_haulno_unlinkable_to_hh             D               HaulNo
#> 3           ca_haulno_tail_mismatch             D               HaulNo
#> 4   icesvocab_key_resolution_hazard             C  HaulValidity, ...
#> 5 datras_field_list_type_divergence             C       Year, SpecCode
```

The registry travels with the data, so a consumer does not need opus's yaml — or
opus at all — to find out that the file it is holding has known caveats.

## Rules that travel with the data

The dictionary carries named definitions — filters, metrics, derived values —
each rendered for both R and SQL, so the same rule can be applied eagerly or
pushed down to the database:

```r
op_definitions("CA")
#>             name   kind             expression                  r
#> 1 linkable_to_hh filter HaulNumber IS NOT NULL !is.na(HaulNumber)
#>                        sql
#> 1 "HaulNumber" IS NOT NULL
```

`op_define()` applies one by name:

```r
op_con("CA") |>
  filter(Survey == "NS-IBTS", Year == 2022, Quarter == 1) |>
  op_define("CA", "linkable_to_hh") |>
  summarise(n = n(), aged = sum(as.integer(!is.na(Age)), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  collect()
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       n  aged
#> 1 45593 15055
```

Under a second over https: the predicate pushes down to parquet row-group
statistics, so only the relevant row groups are fetched.

`linkable_to_hh` is worth reading closely, because it names which CA rows a
haul-level join reaches and is **not** a data-quality filter. The rows it
excludes are attributed to an area rather than a haul; they are a coarser grain,
not bad data, and dropping them silently loses real aged fish.

## Coverage, and the joins

```r
op_surveys()             #> 29 survey acronyms, no live ICES call
op_coverage("HH") |> head(3)
#>   Survey Year Quarter
#> 1   BITS 1991       1
#> 2   BITS 1991       2
#> 3   BITS 1991       3

str(op_relationships("CA"), max.level = 2)
#> $ :List of 5
#>  ..$ left       : chr "CA"
#>  ..$ right      : chr "HH"
#>  ..$ by         : chr [1:8] "Survey" "Year" "Quarter" "Country" ...
#>  ..$ cardinality: chr "many-to-one"
#>  ..$ conflicts  : chr "RecordHeader"
```

The eight-field composite key is the documented way CA and HL reach HH, and
`conflicts` names the column that collides on the join.

## Or take the whole thing as SQL

```r
con <- op_catalog()

DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT column_name, code, label FROM enum_labels
                      WHERE table_name = 'HH' AND column_name = 'Tickler' LIMIT 3")
#>   column_name code                   label
#> 1     Tickler   -9 No ticklers are allowed
#> 2     Tickler    0           Zero ticklers
#> 3     Tickler    1             One tickler

DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM enum_labels")   #> 869
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

`op_catalog()` builds views over the four tables plus `enum_labels` and column
comments, in memory, from the files' own footers — about a second for all four.
There was once a published `catalog.duckdb` alongside the data; it was retired
because a sidecar is one more artifact that can describe a different vintage
than the data beside it. Reconstructing it from the footers cannot drift.

The join that makes the sentinel work legible to someone who knows none of this:

```sql
SELECT h.Tickler, e.label, COUNT(*)
FROM HH h LEFT JOIN enum_labels e
  ON e.table_name = 'HH' AND e.column_name = 'Tickler' AND e.code = h.Tickler
GROUP BY 1, 2
```

`-9 | No ticklers are allowed | 117290`.
